extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, administrative law professors, policymakers, congressional staff, and administrative law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and design criteria for reforming administrative law to reconcile delegation with separation of powers, including a statutory Rulemaking Enabling Act, properly conceived legislative vetoes, and adjustments to executive and judicial oversight of agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept delegation despite original unconstitutionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegation ought to be accepted, even if originally unconstitutional, because the separation of powers is far more critical to the survival of liberty than a firm nondelegation principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article argues accepting delegation is prudent because modern government could not function otherwise; acceptance should be limited to delegation that fits within our long tradition of administrative practice and that does not effectuate a fundamental constitutional change requiring recurrence to the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve separation of powers while accepting delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the nondelegation doctrine is unenforceable, the separation of powers can and should be salvaged through doctrinal adaptation that prevents the blending or concentration of all powers within agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal acceptance of delegation must still maintain limits (e.g., intelligible principle) to avoid agencies combining legislative, executive, and judicial powers in ways that destroy checks and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and apply the intelligible principle constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting delegation does not justify abandoning the 'intelligible principle' standard; Congress should continue to constrain agency discretion by specifying intelligible limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intelligible principle standard remains a useful legal limit on Congress's ability to delegate and helps preserve republican accountability even under a permissive view of delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional supervision of agency lawmaking (conditional delegations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress can and should retain a supervisory role over agency rulemaking by delegating with conditions, including mechanisms for review and withdrawal of consent to proposed rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under a Rulemaking Enabling Act model, Congress may require agencies to present proposed rules and may treat congressional silence as assent while reserving the right to amend or veto—i.e., delegations can include explicit review periods and conditional assent mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative veto constitutional only for legislative acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislative veto should be constitutional when it targets legislative acts (agency actions that are actually lawmaking), but not when it attempts to veto executive or judicial acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies sometimes perform genuinely legislative functions when promulgating rules, Congress can condition delegations to allow a legislative veto of such legislative acts; conversely, vetoing executive or judicial actions would improperly exercise powers not vested in Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model Rulemaking Enabling Act procedural design
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Rules Enabling Act as a model: agencies submit proposed rules to Congress; Congress gets a fixed review period (e.g., seven months) during which it may amend, approve, disapprove, or take no action; if Congress does nothing, the rule becomes law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Rulemaking Enabling Act applying this model across the administrative state would create five constitutionally permissible outcomes (approve/amend + present; approve/amend + President rejects; Congress vetoes; Congress takes no action and President approves or takes ownership; Congress takes no action and President vetoes). The design must ensure compliance with bicameralism and presentment by construing congressional assent appropriately (including assent by silence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameralism and presentment as constitutional constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Any statutory scheme that treats agency rulemakings as becoming law must be consistent with Article I §§1,7 — specifically bicameral passage and presentment to the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemes that treat congressional silence as assent must be structured so that the cumulative statutory process effectively respects Congress's vesting of legislative power and the presentment requirement (e.g., by having the two houses define how 'passage' may occur through delegated processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nature of underlying acts (legislative vs executive vs judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a given administrative action is legislative, executive, or judicial in nature; this classification controls what corrective or review mechanisms are constitutionally available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency action is legislative (rulemaking), Congress may reserve review or veto powers; if executive (individual application of law) or judicial, Congress cannot constitutionally exercise those powers by vetoing them because that would intrude into executive or judicial functions and violate separation of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority over executive functions across agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Under constitutional administration, the President's direct control should extend to all executive functions of the administrative state, regardless of where those functions are exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reconcile a unitary executive with delegated rulemaking oversight, the Article proposes elevating enforcement directors of independent agencies to constitutional officers (Senate-appointed and Presidential-removable) so presidential control over executive functions is coherent with delegated congressional oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial-role reform for high-stakes administrative adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: When interests in life, liberty, or property are implicated, administrative law judges' findings must be submitted as reports and recommendations to Article III judges rather than final decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress can enact this process with statutory precedent modeled on bankruptcy and magistrate judge procedures to preserve Article III judicial authority in the most constitutionally sensitive adjudications while leaving most administrative adjudications undisturbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of veto/override mechanics (timing and thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory design should set clear timeframes (analogous to Article I §7 ten-day presentment window or Rules Enabling Act seven-month review) and define override thresholds (e.g., affirmative two-thirds or silence-as-consent practices) for administrative vetoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several constitutional permutations exist (e.g., congressional affirmative override vs. override by congressional silence); legislators must choose threshold rules consistent with constitutional structure and with predictable political responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve administrative expertise and efficiency while restoring political responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms should retain agencies' technical expertise and flexible administration but shift ultimate political responsibility for legislative questions to the political branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the proposed model most rulemakings would become law by tacit assent and agency expertise remains central; where political choices arise, Congress (and the President) would be required to act affirmatively, thereby clarifying responsibility without wrecking day-to-day agency functioning.
